https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c70g.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Gigantic geoglyphs, known as the Nazca lines, were drawn by people belonging to the Nazca culture, around 1,600 years ago in Peru By Grace Eliza Goodwin Published 1 August 2026 Updated 1 hour ago A small plane carrying tourists has crashed in Peru, killing all 13 people on board, according to local news reports and Peruvian officials. The aircraft, a Cessna Caravan C-208, had been flying over Nazca Lines âarchaeological site when it went down on Saturday. Eleven passengers and two pilots were on board. The passengers included two German, two Spanish and seven Italian tourists, Peru's state news agency reported. The cause of the crash is not yet clear. The Nazca Lines is a popular tourist attraction and Unesco World Heritage site in southern Peru that features ancient drawings of animals in desert sand. Tourists often fly in small planes to see the extent of the drawings. "Given the severity of the accident, there are no survivors. We have recovered four bodies so far," Police Major Jorge Andrade said, according to AFP. The crash happened around 13:00 local time (19:00 BST) in the Pueblo Viejo region after the plane departed from an airport in Pisco, Peru. Video from Reuters news agency shows firefighters spraying water at the scene as smoke rises from the wreckage. In a statement in Spanish posted online by the Municipalidad Provincial de Nasca, officials expressed "deep sorrow" for the accident and extended "heartfelt condolences to the families of the deceased". The statement said the plane belonged to local Peruvian airline Aerodiana. In a statement, the airline said it would "assess its flight schedule in accordance with the directives of the relevant authorities", according to Reuters. The BBC has contacted the airline for comment. This isn't the first plane to crash over the famed site in the past few decades. In 2022, another small tourist plane crashed during a flight over the Nazca Lines site, killing seven on board. And in 2010, a tourist plane went down over the site, killing six people on board. https://patch.com/pennsylvania/doylestow.text: Nearby Communities Warminster, PA New Hope-Lambertville, PA Northampton, PA Hatboro-Horsham, PA Newtown, PA Montgomeryville-Lansdale, PA Upper Southampton, PA Upper Moreland-Willow Grove, PA Upper Dublin, PA Lower Moreland, PA State Edition Pennsylvania National Edition Top National News See All Communities Thank you to our Local Business Sponsor: Community Corner Doylestown Chef Vying To Become Nation's Next "Favorite Chef" The grand prize winner will be determined by a public online vote taking place from now through Thursday at 10 p.m. Jeff Werner , Patch Staff Posted Mon, Aug 3, 2026 at 4:16 am ET | Updated Mon, Aug 3, 2026 at 4:20 am ET (Chef Kelly Unger) DOYLESTOWN, PA — A Doylestown chef is looking for the community’s help as she competes to become the nation’s next “Favorite Chef.” Chef Kelly Unger is one of 16 finalists in the online “Favorite Chef” competition , which brings together seasoned chefs, passionate home cooks, and creative foodies from around the nation for an unforgettable summer showdown of skill, creativity, and heart benefiting the James Beard Foundation, The grand prize winner will be determined by a public online vote taking place from now through Thursday at 10 p.m. Find out what's happening in Doylestown for free with the latest updates from Patch. Everyone gets one free vote every 24 hours. Additional votes can be cast by donating $1 a vote to the James Beard Foundation and its mission and advocacy toward excellence in the independent restaurant industry and leading the country toward a more equitable and sustainable food system. The grand prize winner will be featured in an article appearing in “Taste of Home” magazine, will have the opportunity to cook with Carla Hall on her show, “Chewed Up,” and will win $25,000. Find out what's happening in Doylestown for free with the latest updates from Patch. Story continues below the photos Chef Kelly teaches how to make meatballs in a lemon broth during a Greek cooking class. (Photo courtesy of Chef Kelly Unger) Chef Kelly slices into a Burgundy Epoisse Tart. (Photo courtesy of Chef Kelly Unger) Chef Kelly whips up batter for her nonnettes. (Photo courtesy of Chef Kelly Unger) Chef Kelly, who is well known locally as the director of the Doylestown Farmers Market, was one of more than 20,000 chefs who entered the contest at the beginning of the summer. “I couldn’t have made it this far without the community’s help. Now I need their help once again to push it over the finish line,” she said. “Make Doylestown proud, vote for the hometown girl, and call attention to this beautiful community that I love so much." Click Here To Vote For Chef Kelly Unger. If she wins, Chef Kelly will use her prize money to publish a new cookbook about families cooking together. The funds would pay for expenses not covered by a publisher, including public relations, food photography, and other publishing expenses. Chef Kelly has also entered a parallel competition - the Critic's Pick - which is open to all competitors who make it to the quarterfinals of the Favorite Chef competition. The contestants were invited to submit an hors d'oeuvre or appetizer recipe to the James Beard Foundation. The winner will serve their winning recipe at the prestigious James Beard House to 300 guests at its "Gala for Good" on Nov. 6. For her critic's pick entry, Chef Kelly took a traditional sweet Italian pastry - a Sardinian Pardula - and turned it into a savory hors d'oeuvre. To make it savory, she mixed in roasted mashed sweet potato with the traditional ricotta cheese and saffron filling, added some Rosemary and a touch of orange zest. "The reason I made those flavor choices is that, if I win, I'll be cooking at the Gala For Good on Nov. 6, so I wanted to bring a little bit of Thanksgiving vibe to the dish," said Chef Kelly. Chef Kelly with a batch of her savory Sardinia Pardulas. (Photo courtesy of Chef Kelly Unger) In addition to directing the Doylestown Farmers Market and authoring its newsletter, Chef Kelly serves on the Board of Directors of the Bucks County Foodshed Alliance. She also teaches cooking to 50 three-, four-, and five-year-olds at Maria's House Montessori School in Doylestown. For the past 12 years, Chef Kelly has also taught French, Italian, Greek, and Slovak cooking classes at her studio, The Rooster and The Carrot. And she leads culinary group trips to France, Italy, Greece, and Spain. This fall she's headed to Greece with visits planned to Athens and Crete. Her favorite thing to do in the kitchen is to work with dough, and that includes anything from fresh pasta and pierogies to cream biscuits and a sweet orange and chocolate focaccia. She particularly likes cooking anything from her Slovak heritage, including one of her favorites, stuffed cabbage. “I love our Doylestown community, and it is my privilege to serve it in various ways, especially with my work at the Doylestown Farmers Market. I need help now to make us all proud and call nationwide attention to our amazing, beautiful community,” she said. The winners of both competitions will be announced on September 3. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/25/trum.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday that his US counterpart Donald Trump had informed him that he would grant Ukraine a licence to build coveted Patriot missiles."At our last meeting, President Trump emphasised to me that yes, I have made a final decision. Ukraine will receive licences for the production of Patriot missiles," Zelenskyy said in a voice note to reporters.Zelenskyy and Trump met on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York earlier this week, where the Ukrainian leader said they had discussed potentially "de-escalatory steps that can open up the way to diplomacy.""I am grateful that in the meantime our teams keep working on launching Patriot interceptor production in Ukraine," he added in a post on social media on Tuesday.Kyiv has long called for allies to supply its forces with more interceptors and has been pushing for a licence to produce Patriot missiles domestically, arguing that they are crucial to its ability to defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks.During a meeting with Zelenskyy at the 2026 NATO summit in Ankara, Trump said Washington would give Ukraine a licence to build the missiles."We'll show them how to do it," he said, adding to Zelenskyy: "This way you can't complain that we're not giving them enough."But he appeared to walk back that promise in late July, telling a cabinet meeting that "we have not agreed to that.""We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away that kind of technology," Trump said. “People that you give that technology, they can some day turn on you. You know that is possible".The Patriot missile system is one of the world's most advanced air defences and can reportedly provide area coverage and defence for around 15 to 20 km against incoming ballistic missiles.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text: Listen (4 mins) Save Share Ukraine’s Zelenskyy accuses Russia of violating Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks to the audience via an online video call during the opening ceremony at the Warsaw Security Forum on October 12, 2026, in Warsaw, Poland [Omar Marques/Getty Images] By Al Jazeera Staff , AFP , AP and Reuters Published On 12 Oct 2026 12 Oct 2026 Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of violating the “energy ceasefire” that United States President Donald Trump unilaterally announced at the weekend and promised to respond if the attacks continue. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum via video link on Monday, the Ukrainian leader urged the US to step in to ensure ⁠that Moscow abides by the truce in the four-and-a-half-year Russia-Ukraine war , noting that there have already been “Russian violations of the energy ceasefire announced by ‌President Trump”. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 Trump calls on Ukraine to replace Zelenskyy amid tensions over Russia deal list 2 of 4 Russia’s Yandex says data centre shut down after drone attack list 3 of 4 Oval Office spat to public rebukes: A timeline of Trump-Zelenskyy ties list 4 of 4 Zelenskyy says Russia violated energy truce announced by Trump end of list Zelenskyy said Ukraine was “horribly surprised” that despite Trump’s announcement, Russia struck several energy facilities, including a power plant in Kharkiv. “We are waiting for the details of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, ⁠and we are waiting ⁠to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take,” he said. “This ⁠energy ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step toward ending ‌the war if the Americans truly step in now and make ‌sure ‌Russians respect it … If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond,” Zelenskyy told the Warsaw Security Forum. ⁠On Wednesday, Russia ⁠reportedly struck ⁠a number ⁠of energy facilities in Ukraine’s ‌Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on the ⁠Telegram messaging ⁠app, without ⁠giving ⁠details. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said talks for a possible “energy ceasefire” were ongoing, but rejected Zelenskyy’s proposal for a 60-day truce to allow elections to take place. Advertisement “In the Kremlin, both President Putin and officials at other levels have repeatedly stated we do not want a ceasefire,” Peskov said. “We want long-term peace and are prepared to do everything possible to achieve it.” Trump’s announcement on Sunday that the two countries had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” caused confusion. It came two days after Trump declared a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel, prompting outrage from European allies and Kyiv, who said it would only embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. Both Ukraine and Russia have been launching mutual attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure for months, adding to upward pressure on global energy prices that have risen amid the US-Israel war on Iran. Zelenskyy initially denied any knowledge of the agreement and said it was “news to him”, according to Axios. Trump has previously taken to his Truth Social account to announce truces or other arrangements before either Kyiv or Moscow confirmed them. “An energy ceasefire and other steps to reduce escalation and guarantee security are truly needed here in reality, not just on Truth Social,” Zelenskyy added. European leaders expressed encouragement at the proposed ceasefire, but agreed with Zelenskyy that it had not taken effect. “I have not noted, over‌ the last 48 hours, any energy ceasefire coming from the ‌Russian ‌side,” French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters at a Paris auto show. At the Warsaw Security Forum, ⁠Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “Russia is not interested in ‌a ceasefire, de-escalation, or peace … that is why I will go to Brussels to urge all European partners ⁠to consider increasing ⁠sanctions.” In Brussels, the European Union announced that it has officially added almost 1,600 new sanctions on Russia’s military-industrial complex, including individuals and entities involved in the war, in a bid to maintain pressure on Moscow. “This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas wrote online. “Europe is again showing a united front … We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians.” Meanwhile, Russia ⁠attacked Ukrainian gas production facilities belonging to its state ⁠oil and gas ⁠company Naftogaz in the Kharkiv region overnight, which caused a fire, the ‌company said on Monday. “The attack damaged critical equipment. Our employees are doing everything possible ⁠to repair the ⁠damage as quickly as possible and ⁠prevent risks to ⁠the stable ⁠operation of the energy system,” Naftogaz acting CEO ‌Sergii Fedorenko wrote on Telegram. Advertisement A day earlier, Zelenskyy had said that Ukraine was ready to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceased its own attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
